# How to Turn a Long Podcast Transcript Into Shareable Notes With Claude

> **In short:** You can paste a podcast transcript into Claude and ask for a 5-bullet summary, the best quotes, and an action list — usually in under a minute. You'll need the transcript as text (Claude can't listen to audio), and very long ones may need a paid plan.

A podcast you actually enjoyed drops, and now you want to share the best parts without making your friend sit through 90 minutes. Or you covered it for work and need notes by tomorrow. Here's how to use Claude to turn that wall of text into something a busy person will actually read.

## Before you start
- A Claude account (the free tier works for shorter transcripts; very long ones may need a paid plan)
- Access to **claude.ai** on a web browser or the Claude mobile app
- A transcript of the podcast as plain text — either from the show's website, a transcription service, or your own export
- About 10 minutes total

## Step 1 — Get the transcript as plain text
Before Claude can help, you need the transcript as plain text — words you can copy and paste. Many podcasts publish transcripts on their website or in the show notes. If yours doesn't, run the audio through a transcription service (there are free and paid options) and export the result. A simple .txt or .docx file works best; if you only have a .vtt file with timestamps, that's fine too — Claude can skip past the timecodes. If you only have the audio file and no transcript yet, pause here and get one first; Claude reads text, not sound.
💬 Example: a clean opening line — "Host: Today we're talking about how small teams ship faster than big ones."
You'll know it worked when you have the spoken words sitting in a document or on your clipboard, ready to paste in the next step.

## Step 2 — Open a fresh chat in Claude
Go to **claude.ai** on your computer, or open the Claude app on your phone. Look for a button that starts a brand-new conversation — it usually looks like a pencil icon, a plus sign, or carries a "New chat" label, often near the top-left of the screen. Click or tap it once, and the page clears to an empty conversation with a text box at the bottom. A fresh chat matters because mixing your podcast transcript with old questions can muddle the summary later. If you don't see a clear "new chat" option, try logging out and back in, or closing the browser tab and reopening it.
💬 Example: no typing yet — you're just clearing the deck.
You'll know it worked when the chat shows an empty message thread and a blinking cursor in the input box.

## Step 3 — Paste the transcript and tell Claude what it is
Click into the empty text box, paste the full transcript with your keyboard (Ctrl+V on Windows, Cmd+V on Mac), and then add one short line underneath that explains what you're sharing. That line matters — without it, Claude doesn't know it's looking at a podcast and may try to edit the text as if it were your draft. If your transcript is very long and the paste doesn't fit, look for a paperclip or attachment icon near the text box and upload the file instead; files count toward the same content Claude can read.
💬 Example: after pasting, add this on a new line — "The text above is a podcast transcript. Please read it carefully before I ask my next questions."
You'll know it worked when Claude replies with something like "Got it — I've read the transcript. What would you like to know?" or simply waits for your next instruction.

## Step 4 — Ask for a 5-bullet summary
Stay in the same chat and type a follow-up request for a summary. Ask for a specific number of bullets and a specific audience — vague prompts get vague summaries. Claude usually answers in under a minute for a one-hour transcript, though very long ones may be too much for Claude to read all at once on the free tier. If the answer stops mid-sentence, just reply "keep going" and Claude will resume from where it left off.
💬 Example: "Now please summarize this podcast in exactly 5 bullets for a busy teammate who hasn't listened. Lead with the single most useful idea."
You'll know it worked when you see five short, self-contained bullets that someone could read in 60 seconds and actually understand the episode.

## Step 5 — Pull the best quotes and an action list
Ask for two more things in the same chat: the most quotable lines from the transcript, and a short list of action items — concrete things the listener might actually do after hearing the episode. Ask for them as separate, clearly labeled sections so you can copy each one cleanly. If a quote feels bland, ask for a more surprising or specific one. If the action list sounds generic, ask Claude to tie each item back to a moment in the transcript.
💬 Example: "Now give me two more sections: (1) the 3 most quotable lines, with who said them; (2) a 4-item action list for someone who wants to apply this tomorrow. Label each section clearly."
You'll know it worked when you have three distinct blocks — summary, quotes, action list — that you can copy out separately.

## Step 6 — Save and share the notes
Copy the three blocks out of the chat and paste them into your notes app, an email, or a Slack message. One honest note: every quote Claude pulls is something the speaker actually said in the transcript you gave it — but if you paraphrase a quote before sending, double-check it against the source, because Claude can occasionally mis-attribute a line. If you're on a paid plan, look for a "Share" option that gives your recipient a link to the whole conversation instead. Either approach works — pick the one your teammate will actually open.
💬 Example: "Summary: [paste 5 bullets]. Best quotes: [paste 3 lines]. Action list: [paste 4 items]. Source: [episode name and link]."
You'll know it worked when you hit send and your recipient replies with something other than "what is this?"

## Common mistakes
- **Pasting without telling Claude what the text is.** If you just drop in a transcript and ask "summarize this," Claude may treat it as your own writing and try to edit it. Always add one short line identifying it as a podcast transcript first.
- **Asking for too much in one prompt.** "Summarize this, pull quotes, give me five tweet ideas, and write a LinkedIn post" usually produces shallow output for everything. One clear request per turn gets much better results.
- **Trusting the quotes without checking.** Claude is reading your transcript, so the quotes are real — but if you rewrite them in your own words before sending, you can accidentally change the meaning. For important quotes, copy them verbatim and verify.

## What this means for you
- **In everyday life:** instead of telling a friend "you have to listen to this episode," you can send the three best quotes and one sentence on why it matters — and they will actually read it.
- **For your business or work:** a 90-minute interview becomes a 60-second read for your team in roughly 10 minutes of work, transcribing included.
- **If you're just getting started:** this is one of the easiest first projects with Claude. The transcript gives the assistant a clear job to do, and you'll see useful output within minutes.

## Try it now
Find the transcript of one podcast episode you've already listened to (anywhere from 20 minutes to an hour long), paste it into a fresh Claude chat, and ask for the 5-bullet summary using the prompt from Step 4. That single action is the whole first run — and it usually takes less time than making a cup of coffee.
